source.title: Unintended Memorization of Sensitive Information in Fine-Tuned Language Models
source.authors: Marton Szep; Jorge Marin Ruiz; G. Kaissis; Paulina Seidl; R. von Eisenhart-Rothe; F. Hinterwimmer; D. Rueckert

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling in the provided text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization during fine-tuning in language models, a distinct model family and training setting from the claim versions; its own PII extraction results bear on V1’s memorization/generalization coexistence only indirectly, and it does not test natural-label test generalization.
record.gate_note: The study measures extraction of input-only PII after fine-tuning and compares it with base-model extraction. Those results concern memorization, but the study does not report the natural-label held-out generalization paired with random-label fitting that V1 names. It does not test V2–V8. Prior-work statements about generalization are not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures input-only PII extraction and privacy–utility trade-offs in fine-tuned language models. It cites Feldman and Zhang on memorization supporting generalization but does not test any listed version. In particular, PII extraction alongside downstream performance does not establish V1's random-label fitting and natural-label generalization comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that input-only PII leakage persists after fine-tuning and mitigation. They generally favor post-training methods for privacy–utility trade-offs, while acknowledging stronger DP protection in some settings. Their multi-seed DS results specifically find DP stable, qualifying the broader discussion of DP training instability.
record.recipe_differences: QLoRA fine-tuning of language models on sensitive text with PII extraction attacks; it does not use the random-label or natural-label generalization methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: PII extraction varies with language, prefix length, model architecture and size, dataset, and evaluation mode (greedy, sampling, cross-memorization).

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning changes input-only PII extraction, with increases or decreases depending on dataset, model, PII type, and attack setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning can expose sensitive identifiers absent from training targets, with condition-dependent changes relative to base models.

fits_no_version.finding: The DS frequency analysis reports R² = 0.237 between PII occurrence counts and extraction counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Raw occurrence frequency explains only a limited share of variation in input-only PII extraction.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing LoRA rank from 8 to 64 leaves total extraction counts unchanged in Table 5 while increasing distinct identifiers extracted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional trainable parameters can expand the diversity of extracted PII without increasing total extractions.

fits_no_version.finding: DP, UnDial, DPO, and PII-focused regularization have different leakage, utility, and stability outcomes across datasets, model sizes, and attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Privacy mitigation effectiveness depends on training and evaluation conditions.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study uses three datasets, including synthetic data and private medical datasets; the authors note limits to generalizability and dataset label quality. It primarily evaluates QLoRA models up to 12B parameters. Attack effectiveness varies with prompt construction and evaluation mode; extraction is not a measure of held-out generalization error.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible rows for V1–V8: the paper’s outcomes are PII extraction and task utility, not the behaviors those versions specify. Results described in the supplied text are therefore summarized under fits_no_version rather than treated as rows for the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and paired held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning budgets.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover held-out performance; the reported methods differ in multiple training choices.
Dropout's effect on held-out error; using LoRA dropout and a separate PII-focused regularizer does not test this.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus random examples and retraining to compare test accuracy; targeted unlearning of PII is a different intervention.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the reader's tests/T3 classification to cites_only/T6. Empty rows and labels are appropriate: none of the reported PII or utility results operationalizes V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train on random labels or measure held-out accuracy on natural labels and random labels. Its PII-extraction rates do not test the claimed coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or test-error measurement.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison of held-out task performance.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison under an epoch budget.
No dropout intervention evaluated for held-out error.
No sharpness or other generalization-gap measure.
No removal of memorized training examples followed by a test-accuracy comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
